# Beta blockers

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Relevant pharmacology > Beta blockers*

[Original Article Link](/library/uN0p1g)

---

## Summary

Beta blockers are a group of drugs that inhibit the <u>sympathetic</u> activation of <u>β-adrenergic</u> <u>receptors</u>. Cardioselective blockers (e.g., <u>atenolol</u>, <u>bisoprolol</u>) primarily block <u>β<sub>1</sub> receptors</u> in the <u>heart</u>, causing decreased <u>heart rate</u>, cardiac contractility, cardiac workload, and <u>AVN</u> conduction. Nonselective beta blockers (e.g., <u>pindolol</u>, <u>propranolol</u>) inhibit all <u>β receptors</u> and may cause bronchoconstriction, peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u>, and metabolic imbalances (e.g., <u>hypoglycemia</u> and <u>hyperglycemia</u>, <u>hypertriglyceridemia</u>) in addition to cardiac effects. Cardioselective beta blockers have a lower side-effect profile and are preferred in the management of <u>coronary heart disease</u>, compensated <u>heart failure</u>, <u>acute coronary syndrome</u>, and certain types of <u>arrhythmias</u>. <u>Propranolol</u>, a nonselective beta blocker, is the first-line drug in the management of <u>essential tremor</u>, <u>portal hypertension</u>, <u>migraine prophylaxis</u>, and <u>thyroid storm</u>. Beta blockers are contraindicated in patients with <u>symptomatic bradycardia</u>, <u>AV block</u>, <u>decompensated heart failure</u>, and <u>asthma</u>. Initiation and cessation of beta-blocker therapy should always be gradual to avoid side effects or symptoms of withdrawal (e.g., rebound <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>hypertension</u>, acute <u>cardiac death</u>).




See also “<u>Beta blocker poisoning</u>.”

> [!NOTE]
> With the exception of <u>nebivolol</u>, all cardioselective beta blockers begin with the letters A to M (B<sub>1</sub> = first half of the alphabet). Except for beta blockers with alpha-blocking action (<u>labetalol</u>, <u>bucindolol</u>, <u>carvedilol</u>), all noncardioselective beta blockers begin with the letters N to Z (B<sub>2</sub> = second half of the alphabet).

## Pharmacodynamics

Beta blockers competitively bind to and block <u>β-adrenergic</u> <u>receptors</u>, thereby inhibiting <u>sympathetic</u> (adrenergic and/or noradrenergic) stimulation of <u>β receptors</u>.  See “<u>The sympathetic vs. parasympathetic nervous system</u>” for details regarding the effects of <u>β-adrenergic</u> stimulation.




### Effects of <u>β-adrenergic</u> blockade




| <br>Overview of β-adrenergic blockade [[3]](/library/8nYOEp)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Types of <u>β receptors</u> | Main site of action | Effects of <u>β-adrenergic</u> blockade |
| β<sub>1</sub> | <br>* <u>Heart</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Anti-<u>ischemic</u> effect: β<sub>1</sub> blockade → ↓ <u>heart rate</u> and ↓ cardiac contractility → ↓ blood pressure (BP) and ↓ oxygen consumption by the <u>heart</u> → anti-<u>ischemic</u> effect<br><br>* Antiarrhythmic effect: β<sub>1</sub> blockade → ↓ <u>AVN</u> conduction, ↑ <u>AVN</u> refractory time, and ↓ <u>heart rate</u> → anti-arrhythmic effect<br><br>* Anti-remodeling effect<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Kidneys</u><br><br> | <br>* β<sub>1</sub> blockade of the <u>juxtaglomerular cells</u> → ↓ <u>renin</u> release → ↓ <u>angiotensin II</u> conversion → ↓ H<sub>2</sub>O resorption → ↓ BP<br><br> |  |
| β<sub>2</sub> | <br>* <u>Smooth muscle</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Vasculature: <u>vasoconstriction</u><br><br>* <u>Bronchioles</u>: bronchoconstriction<br><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Ciliary body</u> of the <u>eye</u> [[11]](/library/bNaH-k)<br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Aqueous humor</u> production → ↓ <u>intraocular pressure</u> [[12]](/library/9MYNIp)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Pancreatic beta cells</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Insulin</u> release → <u>hyperglycemia</u> and new-onset <u>diabetes</u>  [[3]](/library/8nYOEp)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Skeletal muscle</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Glucose</u> uptake (↓ <u>insulin</u> <u>sensitivity</u>)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Liver</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ Hepatic <u>glycogenolysis</u> → <u>hypoglycemia</u> (esp. in diabetic patients)<br><br> |  |
| <br>* <u>Lipoprotein lipase</u> enzyme<br><br> | <br>* Inhibits <u>lipoprotein lipase</u> → ↑ <u>triglycerides</u> and ↓ <u>HDL</u> → <u>hyperlipidemia</u><br><br> |  |
| β<sub>3</sub> | <br>* <u>Adipose tissue</u><br><br> | <br>* ↓ <u>Lipolysis</u> → weight gain<br><br> |

Mechanism of action: inotropic drugs




### Intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (<u>ISA</u>) [[6]](/library/ZNaZ-k)[[8]](/library/HnYKup)




* Mechanism of action: <u>partial agonist</u> activity

* Beta blockers with <u>ISA</u> bind to and stimulate the <u>β-adrenergic</u> <u>receptor</u> (agonistic effect) while competitively inhibiting the binding of <u>epinephrine</u> and <u>norepinephrine</u> to <u>β-adrenergic</u> <u>receptors</u> (antagonistic effect).

* Produce partial <u>sympathetic</u> activity while inhibiting the normal and activated <u>sympathetic</u> activity

* Effects

* Cause less <u>bradycardia</u> and less peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u> because of their mild agonistic action

* Have a favorable effect on <u>lipid profile</u> (esp. <u>pindolol</u> and <u>acebutolol</u>): preferred in patients with <u>metabolic syndrome</u>  [[10]](/library/GnYBup)

* Not recommended in patients with <u>congestive heart failure</u>, <u>ischemic heart disease</u>, and <u>tachyarrhythmias</u>  [[13]](/library/YNan-k)

* Agents: <u>pindolol</u>, <u>acebutolol</u>, carteolol, alprenolol [[14]](/library/W7YPkq)





> [!NOTE]
> Beta blockers <u>competitively inhibit</u> adrenergic substances (e.g., <u>adrenaline</u>, <u>noradrenaline</u>) at <u>β receptors</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> A rule to remember the main effector organs for <u>β receptors</u>: There is 1 <u>heart</u> (β<sub>1</sub> blockers act on the <u>heart</u>) and 2 <u>lungs</u> (β<sub>2</sub> blockers affect bronchial <u>smooth muscles</u>).

## Adverse effects

See “<u>Beta blocker poisoning</u>” for features of overdose and their management.




### Overview




| Beta blockers adverse effects |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type of beta blockers | Organ system | Effects |
| <br>Nonselective beta blockers and cardioselective beta blockers  (<u>β<sub>1</sub>-receptor</u> and <u>β<sub>2</sub>-receptor</u> blockade)<br> | Cardiac | <br><br>* <u>Bradycardia</u><br><br>* <u>Bradyarrhythmia</u> (e.g., <u>AV block</u>)<br><br>* <u>Ventricular tachyarrhythmia</u> (<u>torsades de pointes</u>)<br><br>* Worsened <u>heart failure</u> (HF)<br><br>* Worsened vasospasm due to <u>propranolol</u> use<br><br>* <u>Orthostatic hypotension</u> (esp. in elderly patients)  [[15]](/library/1Na2ZO)[[16]](/library/dNaoZO)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>CNS</u>  [[17]](/library/eNaxZO)[[18]](/library/UNab0O)<br> | <br><br>* Fatigue/<u>lethargy</u><br><br>* <u>Sleep disorders</u>, nightmares<br><br>* <u>Depression</u>, <u>hallucinations</u><br><br>* <u>Seizures</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Cutaneous | <br>* <u>Psoriasis</u>  [[19]](/library/qNaCXO)<br><br> |  |
| <br>Nonselective beta blockers  (<u>β<sub>2</sub>-receptor</u> blockade) <br> | Pulmonary | <br>* Bronchoconstriction (esp. patients with <u>asthma</u> and <u>reactive airway disease</u>) <br><br>* <u>Dyspnea</u><br><br>* <u>Bronchospasm</u><br><br>* Exacerbation of <u>asthma</u> and <u>COPD</u><br><br> |
| Peripheral vasculature | <br>* Peripheral <u>vasoconstriction</u><br><br>* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u>  [[20]](/library/tnYXEp)<br><br>* Secondary <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u> [[21]](/library/ygXdBx)<br><br>* Cold extremities<br><br> |  |
| Metabolic | <br><br>* <u>Hypertriglyceridemia</u>, ↓ <u>HDL</u> levels with beta blockers without <u>ISA</u> [[22]](/library/TNa60O)<br><br>* <u>Hyperglycemia</u> and new-onset <u>diabetes</u><br><br>* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>: Beta blockers can mask the <u>sympathetic</u> effects of <u>hypoglycemia</u> (e.g., <u>tachycardia</u>, sweating), leading to dangerous silent (asymptomatic) <u>hypoglycemia</u>.  [[23]](/library/AgXRBx)<br><br>* Weight gain<br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> Beta blockers should be introduced gradually with slow increases in dosage and slowly tapered off when no longer needed.




> [!TIP]
> A number of beta blockers (e.g., <u>metoprolol</u>, <u>carvedilol</u>) are metabolized by <u>CYP2D6</u>. Genetic <u>polymorphisms</u> of <u>CYP2D6</u> (e.g., ultra-rapid metabolization, poor metabolization) can influence adverse effects and tolerated doses. [[24]](/library/_tX5T-)




### Beta-blocker withdrawal




Caused by the sudden termination of beta blockers




* Clinical features

* <u>Tachycardia</u>, <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Acute coronary syndrome</u>, <u>sudden cardiac death</u>  [[25]](/library/NNa-YO)

* Prevention: Taper dose over 7–10 days before discontinuing. [[26]](/library/lNavYO)





We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Indications

### Cardiovascular indications




* <u>Hypertension</u> : beta blockers lower BP by ↓ <u>cardiac output</u> and ↓ <u>renin</u> secretion  [[27]](/library/LNawbO)[[28]](/library/oNa0XO)

* <u>Coronary artery disease</u> 

* <u>Acute myocardial infarction</u> [[29]](/library/KNaUXO)

* Beta blockers should be initiated early in all patients (without contraindications) and continued long-term if tolerated.  [[30]](/library/aSXQyx)

* Beta blockers decrease the size of the <u>infarct</u> and also reduce early and delayed <u>mortality rates</u> in patients with acute <u>MI</u>.

* <u>Angina pectoris</u>: first-line treatment for <u>stable angina pectoris</u> in addition to <u>ACE inhibitors</u> or <u>ARBs</u>  [[27]](/library/LNawbO)[[31]](/library/oz00Fi)

* <u>Heart failure</u>: cardioselective beta blockers (preferred) in combination with <u>ACE inhibitors</u>/<u>ARBs</u> and <u>spironolactone</u> (slows progression of <u>CHF</u>)  [[3]](/library/8nYOEp)[[27]](/library/LNawbO)

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>: <u>atrial flutter</u>, <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>PSVT</u>, VT, and <u>premature ventricular contractions</u> (beta-blockers are <u>class II antiarrhythmic agents</u>; e.g., <u>metoprolol</u>, <u>esmolol</u>, <u>propranolol</u>)  [[32]](/library/6NajXO)[[33]](/library/pNaLXO)





### Specific indications for <u>propranolol</u>




* <u>Essential tremor</u> [[34]](/library/JNasXO)

* <u>Migraine</u> prophylaxis  [[35]](/library/KPaUfk)

* <u>Portal hypertension</u>

* <u>Hyperthyroidism</u> and <u>thyroid storm</u>

* <u>Infantile hemangioma</u>

* <u>Akathisia</u>





#### Miscellaneous




* <u>Hypertensive crises</u>;  (e.g., <u>malignant hypertension</u>): IV <u>labetalol</u> (rapid onset of action)

* <u>Glaucoma</u>: topical beta blockers (<u>timolol</u>, <u>betaxolol</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-induced <u>hypertension</u>: <u>Labetalol</u> is the first-line drug.

## Contraindications

| Contraindications to beta blockers |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Absolute contraindications</u> | <u>Relative contraindications</u> |
| <br><br>* <u>Symptomatic bradycardia</u><br><br>* <u>Cardiogenic shock</u> and <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* <u>Pheochromocytoma</u>: administration of beta blockers before <u>alpha blockers</u> → unopposed α-<u>adrenoceptor</u> mediated <u>vasoconstriction</u> → <u>hypertensive crisis</u> (except nonselective beta blockers with α-<u>antagonism</u>, such as <u>carvedilol</u> and <u>labetalol</u>)<br><br>* <u>Decompensated heart failure</u><br><br>* Combination with <u>calcium channel blockers</u> (<u>diltiazem</u> or <u>verapamil</u>): can precipitate <u>AV block</u><br><br>* <u>Sick sinus syndrome</u> (without a pacemaker); <u>heart block</u> greater than first-degree<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Asthma</u> and <u>COPD</u><br><br>* <u>Psoriasis</u> [[19]](/library/qNaCXO)[[36]](/library/INaYcO)<br><br>* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>, <u>peripheral artery occlusive disease</u><br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u> (except <u>labetalol</u>, which is used to treat <u>pregnancy-induced hypertension</u>)  [[37]](/library/T_06ni)[[38]](/library/rNafcO)<br><br><br> |




We list the most important contraindications. The selection is not exhaustive.
